newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Power supply halved in key part of West Australia.
newsitem.headline: Power supply halved in key part of West Australia.

text.p: A labour dispute had now halved power supplies to Perth and nearby regions of Western Australia but there had been little impact on the key mining sector, industry officials said on Monday.

A spokesman for the state-owned Western Power generation group said the south-west grid, which includes Perth and parts of the Kalgoorlie gold belt, was producing only 1,500 megawatts compared with total capacity of 2,800.

"It (the cuts) would have affected some operations but not all given that a lot of them these days generate their own power," said Western Australia Chamber of Mines and Energy spokesman Tony Johnston.

"It would have had some implications for some operations in the goldfields area and the southwest of the state," said Johnston, who believed the dispute had been well telegraphed, allowing miners to prepare other power sources.
Alcoa's Kwinana alumina refinery, located in the state's southwest, said it had not been affected as it had its own gas/fuel generators.
Western Australia accounts for about 10 percent of Australia's economic output, with all of the nation's iron ore mining from the northwest Pilbara and most of the gold production.

The dispute over the conservative government's industrial relations legislation, now in its seventh day, meant that the 1,040 mw Muja powerstation southwest of Perth was producing only 60 mw with additional power coming from gas allocations from the NorthWest Shelf gas pipeline and electricity purchases from private generators, the Western Power spokesman said.

Power cuts represented a worst case scenario and had been averted so far by industry and households abiding by stiff restrictions which reduced the use of hot water systems, cooking facilities, elevators, air conditioning, and machinery.

"The (state) Chamber of Commerce and Industry have indicated that the losses are about A$120 million (to date) to the Australian economy and we reckon that it has cost us abouty A$6 million for additional fuel and lost sales," Western Power spokesman Peter Winner said.
"We have had a great response in the past week while the restrictions have been on and we have been able to avert any rotational power cuts," Winner said.
"We have not actually had to shed (impose power cuts on) anybody but we have been close on a couple of occasions."

Winner said while Muja was the "baseload" station, other plants in the grid were the 880 mw Kwinana station which was producing at 300 mw on Monday and Bunbury which was producing at about its normal rate of 120 mw.

He said Western Power was seeking orders from the national labour tribunal that striking Muja workers immediately return to work rather than meet their own timetable of resuming operations at 7.00 p.m. (1100 GMT).
